analysis.one_liner: Doubles the federal cigarette tax and equalizes tax rates across all tobacco products.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by Sen. Durbin with 8 Democratic cosponsors, never received a vote and died in the Senate Finance Committee when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would roughly double the federal excise tax on cigarettes, from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand, and raise taxes on every other tobacco product — cigars, pipe tobacco, smokeless products, roll-your-own tobacco, and any new product the FDA classifies as tobacco (such as e-cigarettes) — so they are taxed at rates equivalent to cigarettes. It would also adjust all tobacco tax rates for inflation each year. Higher taxes make tobacco more expensive, which public health research consistently links to lower smoking rates, especially among young people. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a markup or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Public health broadly: higher prices reduce smoking and vaping initiation, particularly among price-sensitive young people, and fewer tobacco-related illnesses over time. Former smokers and nonsmokers benefit from reduced secondhand smoke and lower long-term healthcare costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill roughly doubles the cigarette excise tax, from $50.33 to $100.66 per thousand packs of 20, and doubles the rate for large cigarettes as well [S3].

It equalizes tax rates so that cigars, pipe tobacco, roll-your-own tobacco, smokeless products including nicotine pouches and lozenges, and any FDA-regulated tobacco product are taxed at a per-use rate equivalent to the cigarette tax, closing a loophole where products like roll-your-own tobacco were taxed at a fraction of the cigarette rate [S3].

It applies an annual inflation adjustment to all tobacco tax rates so they do not erode over time, and imposes a floor-stocks tax on inventory held when the increase takes effect so sellers cannot stockpile pre-tax-increase products [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco users, who pay higher prices on every product, and tobacco manufacturers and retailers, who face higher taxes and reduced sales. Excise taxes are passed through to retail prices, and tobacco use is concentrated among lower-income households, so the tax burden falls hardest on lower-income smokers.

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes are passed on to consumers, and because smoking is more common among lower-income people, the doubled cigarette tax would fall disproportionately on lower-income smokers who do not quit, raising their cost of living [S3].

Raising taxes on e-cigarettes and other reduced-risk alternatives at cigarette-equivalent rates, as the bill requires for any FDA-regulated tobacco product, could discourage smokers from switching to less harmful products or push the market toward untaxed illicit sales [S3].
The floor-stocks tax forces retailers and distributors to pay the new rate on existing inventory within 120 days, a cash-flow hit on goods already purchased at the old rate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health case is strong: doubling the cigarette tax and closing the gap between cigarettes and other tobacco products would make all tobacco more expensive, which research shows reduces use, especially among young people. The honest cost is regressive: people who keep smoking — disproportionately lower-income — pay much more, and taxing vaping products at cigarette-level rates may blunt one pathway away from smoking. Whether the health gains outweigh the regressive burden is a real tradeoff, not a clear win.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a markup or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the Tobacco Tax Equity Act of 2019 on September 19, 2019, with eight Democratic cosponsors: Sens. Brown, Markey, Blumenthal, Reed, Hirono, Wyden, Murray, and Merkley [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the committee took no further action on it [S5].
No roll-call vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and vaping companies kept the existing lower tax rates, and smokers avoided a doubling of the federal cigarette tax. No one received the public health benefit the bill's supporters sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies; smokers avoided higher taxes

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill died in a committee chaired by a Republican without any vote being recorded.

industries.note: The bill roughly doubles the cigarette tax and raises rates on every other tobacco product, directly cutting into sales volume in a price-sensitive market. Its interest in the bill ran against the public health goal its supporters cited.

Any FDA-regulated tobacco product would be taxed at a per-use rate equivalent to cigarettes, a far higher rate than most vaping products faced. Vaping companies had a direct financial interest in the bill failing.
The bill imposes a floor-stocks tax on inventory held when rates rise, forcing payment within 120 days on goods bought at the old rate, and higher prices reduce sales volume.
